notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended November 30, 2024, as the county reported them in its Annual Financial Report to the Illinois Comptroller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. The county collector gathers property taxes for every taxing district and pays them over; that money is left out.

Covers the general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service and enterprise (utility) funds. Pension trusts and other fiduciary funds, internal service funds and component units are left out, as are transfers between funds and borrowing.
Capital outlay outside utility funds ($1,598,099) is reported without a function, so it is spread over the county's services in proportion to their spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is bonds, contracts and other long-term debt outstanding at year end (beginning balance plus new debt less debt retired), as reported.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to county board and county office candidates, reported to the State Board of Elections since 2023. Illinois allows business contributions. Individuals, candidates' own money, party and candidate committees, loans and other receipts are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2024, as the township reported them in its Annual Financial Report to the Illinois Comptroller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. Residents also pay Mason County; park, library and fire protection districts are separate governments too.
Illinois townships maintain township roads, assess property and provide general assistance; most also cover the cities and villages inside them.

Covers the general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service and enterprise (utility) funds. Pension trusts and other fiduciary funds, internal service funds and component units are left out, as are transfers between funds and borrowing.
Capital outlay outside utility funds ($125,645) is reported without a function, so it is spread over the township's services in proportion to their spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is bonds, contracts and other long-term debt outstanding at year end (beginning balance plus new debt less debt retired), as reported.

Political money is not scored: no candidates for mayor or village president, council or board, clerk and other local offices of Kilbourne Township reported contributions to the State Board of Elections since 2023.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.
Cameras: no license-plate cameras are mapped inside Kilbourne Township's borders in OpenStreetMap as of 2026-10-18.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Illinois yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
